title: Inquest date set for Hamilton man shot dead by police
subtitle: Jason Peterson, 42, died after officers shot him twice in the head in July 2020.
article: A coroner's inquest into the police shooting death of a 42-year-old Hamilton man is set to begin next month.
In a release Tuesday, Dr. Karen Schiff, supervising coroner for the region, said the Nov. 4 inquest into Jason Peterson's death is expected to last five days and hear from roughly 15 witnesses.
Peterson died in hospital July 8, 2020, a day after an interaction with police in the parking lot of a Cannon Street East convenience store ended with him shot twice in the head.

Hamilton police had been tracking the father of two for about a half-hour prior to the shooting in front of Corner's Variety around 4 p.m. on July 7, according to Ontario's police watchdog, which probes all police-involved shootings that result in death or injury.

In a March 2021 report, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) said police responded to an Ottawa Street North residence around 3:30 p.m. for reports of a man allegedly holding a shotgun to his ex-girlfriend's head.

Police located the suspect - later confirmed to be Peterson - in a gold sedan parked in the convenience store lot at Cannon and Gage Avenue North. He was seen briefly entering the shop and buying some Gatorade.

Video surveillance previously obtained by the Spec showed it wasn't 40 seconds from the time Peterson exited the front door of Corner's Variety and entered the passenger seat of the sedan that two uniformed officers jumped out of a rolling cruiser and drew their guns toward him.

The SIU said in its report Peterson fired a shotgun in the direction of an officer who'd grabbed the driver's left arm. Two officers then fired one round apiece at Peterson's head, according to the watchdog, which ultimately cleared Hamilton police of wrongdoing and said its members had "little option other than to return fire."
Peterson was remembered by his mother and daughter as a loving family man, always smiling, with a penchant for cooking, camping and spending time with those close to him.
The inquest into the circumstances around his death is mandatory under Ontario's Coroners Act. A jury will make recommendations aimed toward preventing further deaths.
